Definition: The largest artery in the abdomen, supplying blood to the lower body; located in the retroperitoneum and prone to aneurysms or occlusion.
An abnormal whooshing sound heard over the abdomen due to turbulent blood flow, often indicating arterial stenosis or aneurysm.
A Doppler measurement used in renal artery evaluation; values less than 3 m/s² suggest stenosis by indicating delayed systolic upstroke.
Time from onset of systole to peak velocity in Doppler waveforms; greater than 70 ms indicates proximal stenosis (e.g., tardus parvus pattern).
Sudden reduction in blood flow to tissues, often due to emboli or thrombosis, leading to pain, pallor, and potential tissue death.
Death of tubular cells in the kidney, the most common cause of immediate postoperative renal transplant failure, often due to ischemia.
An artifact in Doppler ultrasound where high velocities appear wrapped around the spectrum, mimicking reversed or low flow.
Transient monocular vision loss due to temporary ischemia in the retinal artery, often a hemispheric symptom of carotid disease.
A non-invasive test comparing ankle and brachial systolic pressures; normal range 0.9-1.3, lower values indicate peripheral arterial disease.
A deep vein in the lower leg accompanying the anterior tibial artery; often paired and drains the anterior compartment.
Congenital narrowing of the aorta, causing hypertension in the upper body and decreased femoral pulses, often with abdominal bruit.
Blockage or narrowing of the aorta and iliac arteries due to atherosclerosis, leading to claudication or blue toe syndrome.
Abnormal connection between an artery and vein, causing high-flow shunting; can be post-biopsy or dialysis-related, with low-resistance waveforms.
Buildup of plaque in arteries, leading to narrowing or occlusion; common cause of peripheral arterial disease and ulcers.
Increase in venous Doppler signal with distal compression (e.g., calf squeeze), used to assess patency and rule out obstruction.
A thoracic vein that drains into the superior vena cava; can serve as collateral in central venous obstruction.
Embolization of atheromatous debris to toes, causing painful blue discoloration; associated with aortoiliac disease.
Deep vein in the upper arm accompanying the brachial artery; typically paired and joins to form the axillary vein.
Major vein formed by confluence of subclavian and internal jugular veins; drains upper body and can be obstructed in thoracic outlet syndrome.
Obstruction of hepatic veins or IVC, leading to liver congestion; not typically associated with tumor invasion.
Inflammatory disease affecting small arteries/veins in smokers, often involving distal vessels like posterior tibial artery.
Surgical conduit (e.g., vein or synthetic) to reroute blood around occluded arteries; monitored with duplex for patency and stenosis.
Surgical removal of plaque from the carotid artery to prevent stroke; post-op changes include bulb size alterations.
Major branch of abdominal aorta supplying foregut; velocities increase post-meal normally, but can be compressed in median arcuate syndrome.
Narrowing of the celiac artery, causing turbulent flow; differentiated from compression syndromes via breathing maneuvers.
Blockage in major proximal arteries, leading to altered flow patterns like high resistive in distal branches.
Blockage in major veins like SVC or brachiocephalic, causing edema and collateral veins; common in AVF patients with arm swelling.
Superficial vein on the lateral upper arm/forearm; drains into axillary vein and used in AVF creation.
Leg pain from peripheral arterial disease relieved by rest; first symptom of chronic lower extremity occlusive disease.
Alternative pathways that develop around occlusions; typically more numerous, tortuous, and smaller than native vessels.
Major vein at groin level; assessed for phasicity and augmentation to detect iliac or femoral obstruction.
Increased pressure within muscle fascial compartments, causing ischemia; due to swelling, not atherosclerosis.
Full arterial loop in hand connecting radial and ulnar arteries; patency tested with PPG and compression.
Ultrasound test where veins are compressed transversely; lack indicates thrombosis or incompressibility.
Non-phasic, steady flow signal; indicates proximal venous obstruction (e.g., brachiocephalic or SVC).
Imaging plane dividing body into front/back; not standard for vein compressibility (transverse is preferred).
Bluish discoloration due to low oxygen; seen in Raynaud's after pallor phase or in blue toe syndrome.
Blood clot in deep veins, causing secondary venous insufficiency; history can lead to reflux.
Nerve damage from diabetes, causing foot issues but not directly blue toe syndrome.
Blood flow during heart relaxation; increased in low-resistance beds or AVFs.
Ultrasound combining B-mode imaging and Doppler for vascular assessment; used post-endarterectomy or for veins/arteries.
Difficulty speaking, a hemispheric symptom from carotid territory ischemia.
Sharp upstroke in Doppler waveform; normal in renal segmental arteries, indicating no proximal stenosis.
Clots or debris traveling in bloodstream; main cause of acute lower extremity ischemia or blue toe.
See "Carotid endarterectomy"; general term for plaque removal from arteries.
Symptom of superior vena cava syndrome or central obstruction, with edema and dyspnea.
Deep vein in thigh; assessed for reflux or obstruction; valves are numerous here.
Nonatherosclerotic arterial disease causing beading/narrowing; commonly affects distal internal carotid or renal arteries.
Lower medial leg region where venous ulcers often occur due to insufficiency.
Tissue death from ischemia; potential complication of compartment syndrome.
Calf muscle; can compress popliteal artery in entrapment syndromes.
Long superficial leg vein; common source of reflux in venous insufficiency.
Localized blood collection; post-biopsy complication but not typically with low-resistance flow.
Weakness on one body side; hemispheric symptom from carotid ischemia.
Drains liver to IVC; normal flow is hepatofugal, pulsatile due to cardiac influence.
Clot in hepatic veins; causes Budd-Chiari-like symptoms but not aliasing post-biopsy.
Liver cancer; can invade veins but less commonly IVC than renal cell carcinoma.
Flow away from the liver; normal for hepatic veins, abnormal for portal vein (indicates portal hypertension).
Flow toward the liver; normal for portal vein, abnormal for hepatic veins.
System involving portal and hepatic veins; normal portal flow is hepatopetal, non-pulsatile; hepatic is hepatofugal, pulsatile.
Waveform with little diastolic flow; seen in muscular arteries or proximal to occlusion.
Partial hand arterial loop; causes no PPG change with radial compression if ulnar is occluded.
Blockage of artery supplying an AVF; causes reduced flow but not edema.
Major vein returning blood from lower body to heart; invaded by tumors like renal cell carcinoma; few valves.
Another name for brachiocephalic vein.
Major neck vein draining brain; obstruction doesn't cause continuous subclavian flow.
External pressure on vessels; not typical for blue toe but seen in syndromes like median arcuate.
Swelling on same side as AVF; indicates central venous obstruction.
Aortoiliac occlusion causing buttock claudication, impotence; not related to celiac compression.
Peritoneal space; not location of abdominal aorta.
Absence of respiratory variation in venous Doppler; indicates proximal obstruction (e.g., partial iliac).
High diastolic flow; normal in brain/renal arteries or post-exercise; seen in AVFs.
Skull bone behind ear; not a transtemporal landmark for TCD.
Compression of celiac axis by median arcuate ligament; velocities change with breathing.
Inner ankle bone; PPG sensor placement above it for venous insufficiency testing.
Hardening of artery inner wall; associated with monophasic waveforms and high ABI (>1.3) in diabetics.
Distal segment of MCA; landmark in transcranial Doppler for cerebral flow assessment.
Single-phase waveform; indicates severe disease or calcification in arteries, or obstruction in veins.
Space between liver and kidney; not aorta location.
Original anatomical arteries/veins; compared to collaterals or grafts.
Entrapment of vessels/nerves; e.g., thoracic outlet, causing decreased pulses.
Vessel narrowing not due to plaque; e.g., fibromuscular dysplasia or Takayasu arteritis.
Symptom from vertebrobasilar insufficiency, like syncope, not lateralized like hemiparesis.
Angled imaging plane; not standard for vein compression.
Ovarian cancer; can invade veins but less commonly IVC.
Effort thrombosis of axillary/subclavian vein; confirmed with upper extremity venous duplex; causes arm edema.
Paleness; initial phase in Raynaud's disease due to vasospasm.
Arterial network in palm; completeness tested with PPG and artery compression.
Openness of a vessel or graft; assessed via Doppler flow or compression.
Chest muscle; compresses axillary vessels in some thoracic outlet cases.
Connects superficial to deep veins; responsible for reflux if thigh tourniquet normalizes refill time.
Relating to the peritoneum cavity; not aorta location.
Deep calf vein; often singular in lower extremity venous system.
Flow varying with respiration; normal in veins, lost with obstruction.
Non-invasive test using light to measure blood volume changes; used for venous insufficiency or arterial patency in digits.
Vein behind knee; numerous valves; obstruction doesn't affect CFV augmentation if proximal.
Carries blood from gut to liver; normal flow hepatopetal, non-pulsatile; occlusion causes high resistance.
Blockage of portal vein; not typically with aliasing post-liver biopsy.
Brain artery; distal segment used as landmark in TCD.
Deep calf vein accompanying posterior tibial artery; often paired.
Valve incompetence without prior thrombosis; causes include congenital absence or damage.
Deep thigh vein; complete occlusion doesn't cause CFV phasicity loss.
Throbbing waveform synced to heartbeat; normal in arteries, abnormal in portal vein (indicates hypertension).
Vasospasm of digits triggered by cold/stress, causing pallor, cyanosis, rubor; tested with PPG.
Transplanted kidney; common complication is renal artery stenosis.
Supplies kidney; lowest resistive index among options; stenosis causes tardus parvus in segments.
Narrowing of renal artery; most common vascular issue in transplants.
Clot in renal artery; less common than stenosis in allografts.
Kidney cancer; most common to invade IVC via renal vein.
Narrowing of renal vein; rare in transplants.
Clot in renal vein; can occur post-transplant but less common.
Measure of vascular resistance (PSV - EDV)/PSV; lowest in renal arteries (low-resistance bed).
Space behind peritoneum where abdominal aorta and IVC lie.
Imaging plane dividing body into left/right; used in vascular ultrasound but not for compression.
Size of Doppler gate; too large can cause artifacts in graft imaging.
Thigh muscle; not common in thoracic outlet compression.
Neck muscle; most frequent compressor in thoracic outlet syndrome.
Intrarenal branches; waveforms assess for proximal stenosis (e.g., acceleration time).
Superficial posterior leg vein; can cause reflux but less than great saphenous.
Ultrasound mode showing velocity spectrum over time; used for waveforms in hepatic/portal veins.
Skull bone; landmark in transtemporal TCD window.
Diversion of blood to AVF causing distal ischemia; not primary cause of edema in AVF patients.
Supplies midgut; high resistance when fasting, decreases post-meal.
Major vein to right atrium; obstruction causes facial/upper edema, continuous subclavian flow.
Obstruction of SVC causing upper body edema, dyspnea; often from malignancy.
Fainting; nonhemispheric symptom indicating vertebrobasilar insufficiency.
Inflammatory vasculitis affecting large arteries like brachiocephalic; predominantly in young females.
Delayed (tardus) and reduced (parvus) systolic peak in waveforms; indicates proximal stenosis.
Compression of neurovascular bundle at neck/shoulder; causes arm symptoms, confirmed with upper extremity duplex.
Ultrasound through skull windows (e.g., transtemporal) to assess cerebral arteries like MCA.
Skull window over temple for TCD to evaluate middle cerebral artery.
Cross-sectional imaging plane; standard for assessing vein compressibility.
Three-phase arterial waveform (forward, reverse, forward); normal in peripheral arteries.
Heart valve between right atrium and ventricle; overfilling before opening seen in hepatic vein waveforms.
Extension of cancer into vessels; e.g., renal cell carcinoma into IVC.
Forearm artery; occlusion with incomplete palmar arch shows no PPG change on radial compression.
Dilated, tortuous vein; PPG sensor not placed over it for insufficiency testing.
Inability of veins to return blood; primary from valve damage, secondary from DVT; tested with refill time and PPG.
Time for vein refilling after compression; normalizes with tourniquet if perforator reflux.
Backward flow in veins due to incompetent valves; assessed with Doppler and tourniquets.
Structures preventing backflow; most numerous in calf veins like popliteal.
Ultrasound of vertebral/basilar arteries; indicated for nonhemispheric symptoms like syncope.
Shape of Doppler signal; e.g., monophasic in disease, triphasic normal.
